name: The Hookman
description: A classic American urban legend in which a couple parked at a lovers' lane flee from a radio-warned escaped killer with a hook for a hand and find his hook torn off and dangling from the car door handle.
full_description: The Hookman (also called 'The Hook' or 'The Hook Man') is a classic American urban legend that began circulating in the 1950s and was widely told among teenagers by 1959. In its standard form, a young couple is parked at a remote lovers' lane when a radio bulletin announces that a dangerous prisoner — variously a serial killer or escaped patient from a mental institution — has just escaped, identifiable by a hook in place of one hand. The girl insists they leave; the boy reluctantly drives off. When they arrive home and the boy walks around to open her door, they find a bloody hook hanging from the handle. The legend was first published, so far as documented, in the 'Dear Abby' advice column on 8 November 1960, and was treated as a foundational example by folklorists including Jan Harold Brunvand, who placed it at the centre of his 1981 The Vanishing Hitchhiker. Folklorists have read the legend as a coded warning to teenagers about isolated places and adolescent sexuality (Alan Dundes), as a contest between conventional and deviant social actors (Bengt af Klintberg), and as a moralistic 'custodian' tale (Bill Ellis). The Hookman has been a recurring template in modern horror cinema and television, including a hook-wielding killer in I Know What You Did Last Summer (1997) and episodes of Supernatural and Community.
origin: American urban legend with countless local variants throughout the contiguous United States; the legend has also circulated in Canada and the United Kingdom.

etymology.origin: American English. The character is identified by his prosthetic hook in place of a hand; 'hookman' is a descriptive nickname rather than a proper name.
etymology.meaning: 'The man with the hook'; a hook-handed killer character in an urban-legend script.
etymology.first_use: Circulating orally in the United States from the early-to-mid 1950s; first documented in print in 1960 in the 'Dear Abby' newspaper column.

timeline.event: By 1959, the Hookman story is described by folklorists as widespread among American teenagers
timeline.significance: Marks the legend's transition from local oral story to nationally distributed urban legend
timeline.source: Jan Harold Brunvand, The Vanishing Hitchhiker (1981), citing earlier oral evidence

timeline.event: First documented printed version of the Hookman legend appears in the 'Dear Abby' column, attributed to a reader 'Jeanette'
timeline.significance: Earliest fixed printed version of the legend

timeline.event: Jan Harold Brunvand publishes The Vanishing Hitchhiker, treating the Hookman as a foundational case study of urban legend
timeline.significance: Anchors the legend in academic folklore
timeline.source: Brunvand, J. H. (1981), The Vanishing Hitchhiker

timeline.event: Alvin Schwartz publishes Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark, with a Hookman story
timeline.significance: Carries the legend to a generation of American children in print
timeline.source: Schwartz, A. (1981), Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark

timeline.event: I Know What You Did Last Summer is released in US cinemas, featuring a hook-wielding killer overtly based on the legend
timeline.significance: Fixes the Hookman as a cinematic horror template
timeline.source: I Know What You Did Last Summer (Columbia Pictures, 1997)

cultural_notes: Generally told as a 'true story that happened to a friend of a friend', with the irony of its evident folkloric structure usually invisible to the original tellers.
